channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: Evidence against your belief makes you hold tighter.
item.description: Belief perseverance is the cognitive tendency to maintain a position even when the evidence supporting it has been clearly debunked.

item.title: You judge inaction more leniently than harmful action.
item.description: The omission bias is the tendency to view harmful inaction as less morally wrong than harmful action with the same outcome.

item.title: Asking for your plan makes you likely to follow it.
item.description: The mere measurement effect describes how measuring intentions can influence behavior, though the outcome depends on the frequency of questioning.

item.title: Your chances of success rise after a blatant refusal.
item.description: The door-in-the-face technique demonstrates that you are more likely to agree to a small request after rejecting a larger, unreasonable one.

item.title: One visible flaw blinds you to everything else.
item.description: The horns effect is the negative manifestation of the halo effect, a phenomenon first described by Edward Thorndike in his 1920 paper 'A Constant Error in Psychological Ratings.'

item.title: You reject good ideas because you did not create them.
item.description: The 'not-invented-here' bias causes people to devalue external solutions in favor of internal ones.

item.title: You think of future plans in impossible terms.
item.description: Construal level theory explains that the more distant an event is, the more abstractly you represent it.

item.title: You might be misreading your fear as attraction.
item.description: The misattribution of arousal occurs when your brain misidentifies the source of physiological excitement.

item.title: You work significantly faster as you approach a goal.
item.description: The goal gradient effect shows that the closer you are to finishing a task, the more effort you invest to complete it.

item.title: Competence is more likeable when it is slightly flawed.
item.description: The pratfall effect is the tendency for a mistake to increase the attractiveness of an already highly competent person, while a mistake by an average or incompetent person tends to make them less attractive.

item.title: You mirror the physical behaviors of the person you like.
item.description: The chameleon effect is the unconscious imitation of a conversation partner's posture, gestures, and facial expressions.

item.title: You consume more when portion sizes are labeled as units.
item.description: The unit bias explains why people eat or use more when a quantity is presented as a single item.

item.title: You remember facts better if you explain them yourself.
item.description: The generation effect demonstrates that information is better retained when you produce it from your own mind.

item.title: You subconsciously blame victims to preserve your sense of order.
item.description: The just-world hypothesis is the tendency to believe that people get what they deserve, even in cases of random misfortune.

item.title: You accept generic personality descriptions as uniquely accurate.
item.description: In a 1949 study, students completed a personality test and were given a feedback report, which was identical for all participants.

item.title: You value your own possessions more than the market does.
item.description: In a 1990 experiment, participants demanded more money to sell a mug they were given than they were willing to pay to acquire it.

item.title: One new purchase triggers a cycle of constant upgrades.
item.description: The Diderot effect describes how a single acquisition often leads to a spiral of consumption.

item.title: You assign human traits to inanimate geometry.
item.description: In a 1944 study, viewers who watched an animation of shapes moving around a box almost universally described the shapes as having distinct, anthropomorphic personalities.

item.title: You invent memories to fill missing gaps.
item.description: In a 1995 study by Loftus and Pickrell published in Psychiatric Annals, 25% of participants reported memories of being lost in a mall after researchers presented them with a false story as if it were provided by their family.

item.title: You ignore how long an ordeal actually lasted.
item.description: When rating the discomfort of a medical procedure, patients disproportionately weigh the peak pain and the pain at the very end.

item.title: You help less when others are present.
item.description: A 1968 study found that participants were significantly slower to report a plume of smoke filling a room if they were in a group compared to when they were alone.

item.title: You accept the pre-selected option far too often.
item.description: In Germany (opt-in), 12% of the population have registered as donors, while in Austria (opt-out), 99% are classified as potential donors by default.

item.title: A small request makes you agree to more.
item.description: A 1966 study found that homeowners were four times more likely to agree to a large, ugly sign in their yard if they had previously agreed to a small, inconsequential request.

item.title: You filter out information that challenges your beliefs.
item.description: A 1979 study found that when shown opposing studies on capital punishment, people rated evidence confirming their view as credible and dismissed contradictory evidence as flawed.

item.title: You keep reading this book because you started.
item.description: Investing time or money in a failing venture makes you paradoxically more likely to continue investing further.

item.title: A random number changes what you pay today.
item.description: In a 1974 study, people asked if the percentage of African nations in the UN was higher or lower than 10% guessed lower than those asked if it was higher or lower than 65%.

item.title: You believe common causes of death are much rarer.
item.description: People consistently overestimate the frequency of dramatic deaths like shark attacks while underestimating common, quiet ones like strokes.

item.title: Your choice depends entirely on how options are phrased.
item.description: In the 1981 study, 72% of participants chose a certain outcome of saving 200 out of 600 lives over a risky option with a 1/3 probability of saving everyone.

item.title: Everyone follows a rule that no one actually likes.
item.description: A 1993 study found that students privately disliked campus drinking but believed peers enjoyed it.

item.title: You prefer associating with winners to signal your status.
item.description: A 1976 study found students wore more university gear the day after their football team won.

item.title: You remember things better when they relate to you.
item.description: A 1977 study found people recall adjectives significantly better when they judge them against their own traits.

item.title: You believe your effort influences random outcomes.
item.description: A 1975 study found people bet more on lottery tickets when they selected the numbers themselves.

item.title: Your memories are rewritten by questions asked after the event.
item.description: The misinformation effect demonstrates that memory is a reconstructive process, and post-event information can significantly alter the accuracy of eyewitness reports.

item.title: You believe your future is better than your present.
item.description: The optimism bias is a persistent cognitive error where you underestimate the likelihood of negative events and overestimate the likelihood of positive ones.

item.title: Your brain confuses ease of processing with actual truth.
item.description: The fluency heuristic leads people to believe that information is true simply because it is easy to understand or recall.

item.title: You reshape your own memory to justify your past decisions.
item.description: Hindsight bias allows you to believe that past events were more predictable than they actually were at the time.

item.title: You will choose the forbidden option just to feel free.
item.description: Psychological reactance is the drive to reclaim your sense of autonomy when you feel a choice is being restricted.

item.title: Rewarding a behavior you enjoy will make you quit.
item.description: The overjustification effect occurs when external incentives decrease your intrinsic motivation to perform an activity.

item.title: You are remarkably poor at predicting your future emotions.
item.description: The affective forecasting error demonstrates that people consistently overestimate the intensity and duration of their future emotional states.

item.title: You judge the quality of a choice by its outcome.
item.description: Outcome bias is the tendency to evaluate the intelligence of a decision based on the final result rather than the quality of the process used to make it.

item.title: You prefer things to stay exactly as they are.
item.description: Status quo bias describes a preference for the current state of affairs, even when changing it would provide a clear advantage.

item.title: You mistakenly believe others think exactly like you do.
item.description: The false consensus effect is the cognitive bias where you overestimate the extent to which your opinions and habits are shared by others.

item.title: You like people more when you live near them.
item.description: The propinquity effect is the tendency for people to form friendships with those they encounter in their daily physical environment.

item.title: You create obstacles to explain away your future failures.
item.description: Self-handicapping occurs when you intentionally place hurdles in your own path to protect your ego.

item.title: Your brain prioritizes bad news over good news.
item.description: A 2001 review confirmed that negative events, emotions, and interactions have a greater impact on your psychological state than neutral or positive ones.

item.title: You like things more simply because you saw them before.
item.description: In a 1968 study, participants rated random shapes and words as more appealing the more frequently they were exposed to them.

item.title: You judge your behavior by your circumstances, not character.
item.description: Jones and Nisbett (1971) proposed the actor-observer asymmetry hypothesis, though subsequent meta-analyses have found little evidence that this behavior is a reliable or consistent psychological phenomenon.

item.title: A third option changes what you choose entirely.
item.description: A 1982 study found that adding a clearly inferior third option increases the likelihood that people will choose the original preferred option.

item.title: You become less careful when you feel safer.
item.description: Peltzman's 1975 study argued that mandatory automobile safety regulations did not lead to the predicted decrease in aggregate traffic fatality rates because drivers engaged in offsetting risky behavior.

item.title: New experiences make time feel like it's slowing.
item.description: Initial studies suggested an unexpected stimulus makes its duration appear 30–50% longer, though later research shows the effect is generally around 10% or less.
